title: Preemptible reserve lanes: adaptive throttling, surge-window accounting, and invoice smoothing
creator: Maya Chen
description: Design and implement a preemptible reserve lane feature for Dedicated customers that provides short-duration burst capacity with adaptive throttling and a predictable invoice-smoothing policy. The goal is to allow controlled temporary boosts without surprising overage invoices while preserving latency SLOs for committed traffic.
background: Customers request occasional short bursts above their reserved throughput for traffic spikes (campaign launches, batch jobs). Current 'surge pool' implementations either 1) allow bursts that feed straight into overage billing (surprising invoices) or 2) deny bursts and harm UX. We need a middle ground: a preemptible reserve lane with transparent accounting (surge-window) and an invoice smoothing policy that amortizes small short bursts into reserves where reasonable.
proposed_solution: Introduce a Preemptible Reserve Lane (PRL) construct: 1) Each Dedicated allocation exposes a configurable PRL capacity (tokens/sec) and a burst window (seconds). 2) Incoming requests are scored as committed vs preemptible based on customer config and current utilization. 3) PRL is subject to adaptive throttling: when physical fleet pressure is high, PRL is gradually degraded by reclaiming batches with oldest start times first (fairness across customers). 4) Accounting: PRL consumption is tracked in a time-window ledger (surge-window) which supports invoice smoothing rules (threshold-based amortization and one-off credits). 5) Controls: Host operators can mark fleet pressure modes (normal, constrained, emergency) which change PRL reclaim aggressiveness and notification levels.
acceptance_criteria: Configurable PRL exposed in Dedicated config and Console: capacity, window, and enable/disable
Runtime scoring differentiates committed vs PRL requests with <1ms median decision latency
Adaptive throttling reclaims PRL traffic according to policy and maintains 99th percentile latency SLO for committed traffic
Accounting ledger records PRL usage per minute and supports queries for last 30 days
Billing pipeline accepts PRL ledger and applies invoice-smoothing policy: auto-amortize bursts under X tokens/min into monthly reserve; generate credit if burst violates policy
Operator controls to escalate fleet mode and observe immediate PRL reclaim metrics in Console
End-to-end integration tests and a canary on a single POOL for 72 hours with synthetic bursts pass
architecture_notes: PRL decisions are best implemented as a lightweight admission layer in the serving gateway, before batching. Ledger events should be appended to the existing usage-event stream with a PRL flag to reuse existing billing ingestion. Reclaim decisions emit trace events for debugging. We will reuse the smart-routing signal to prefer cheaper model variants when reclaiming preemptible tokens.

metrics: PRL_utilization_percent: percentage of configured PRL capacity used (per-pool)
Committed_p99_latency: p99 latency for committed traffic (target no regression)
PRL_reclaim_rate: tokens/sec reclaimed under constrained mode
Billing_delta_per_customer: difference between baseline invoice and post-PRL invoice (30d)
Customer_support_mentions: number of support tickets referencing PRL or burst billing
risks: Customers misunderstand PRL semantics leading to support escalations — mitigated by clear Console copy and email opt-in
Billing pipeline mis-attribution causing incorrect invoices — mitigation: shadow billing run and manual reconciliation before auto-bill
Performance overhead at gateway adds latency — mitigation: microbenchmark scoring code and deploy behind feature flag
Operator misuse of fleet pressure modes could lead to unnecessary widespread reclaiming — mitigation: RBAC for fleet mode toggles and audit logs
open_questions: What should the default invoice-smoothing thresholds be? (proposal: amortize bursts < 2x reserved throughput sustained for < 10 minutes)
Should PRL be tenant-configurable by default or only enabled per-enterprise contract?
Do we need hard caps on total PRL across a region to avoid large correlated bursts?
How to present PRL usage on invoices so customers can reconcile easily?
